title: A value handed to a program as a positional argument is re-read as an instruction because it starts with a dash
index_line: T-0036 · EXEC · a username reaches a positional argv slot; the receiver treats a leading dash as a transport directive · c/rust/go/java/python · corroborated
invariant_violated: A caller assumes that an argument placed after the options is data, because it is in a positional slot. But the receiving parser has a legacy rule for positionals that begin with a dash, and a username is attacker-chosen text — so 'positional' is a convention, not a guarantee, and one dash re-enters the option grammar.

mechanism.does: the attacker connects to the exposed service and supplies a value the front end will pass on as a positional argument
the front end assembles an argv and execs the backend program, placing the attacker's value in a slot that comes after the flags
the backend parser sees the value begins with a dash and applies its option/transport syntax instead of treating it as a name
the selected directive makes the backend read its *trusted* login parameters from a channel the attacker controls

attacker-supplied fields replace the identity and policy values the front end intended to pass, so the session is granted the privileges it asked for — the authorization outcome follows the attacker's parameters
the session escalates from read-only to full control of the device

source.protocol.value: a login field of a network service (SSH username, telnet/MAC field, RADIUS username) — a value the caller assumes is inert because it is 'just a name'

sink.exec.noshell.value: the exec/execv of a helper program whose argv is built from the request — argument injection, no shell involved

encoding.shell.value: a leading dash, and the directive letters the backend understands; nothing else is needed

guard.none.value: no `--` separator between options and positionals, and no validation that the value cannot begin with a dash

preconditions.expr: a privileged front end builds an argv containing request-derived values
the parser of the exec'd program accepts dash-prefixed positionals as directives

check.spec: call the helper directly with a dash-prefixed positional and see whether it changes behaviour instead of being treated as a name

preconditions.expr: the value is attacker-chosen (a username or label) and not constrained to a safe character class

success: a username that begins with a dash changes the session's privileges rather than failing to authenticate
the backend reads its parameters from a channel the attacker supplied (a pty, a pipe, a file descriptor) instead of the front end
a read-only session becomes a full one without any credential change
failure_like: the caller inserts `--` before positionals, or rejects values starting with `-`
the backend has no dash-directive grammar for positionals
false_positive: an authentication failure for a dash-prefixed username — that is the safe behaviour; the bug needs a directive the parser accepts
privilege change caused by the credentials supplied, not by the argument — control for this with a benign dash value

hazards: argument injection is not command injection: metacharacters are irrelevant and the payload is a flag. Check for `--` before blaming quoting
the value crosses a process boundary, so the interesting parser is in the *next* binary — read its option grammar
legacy transports (read-your-parameters-from-fd-N) are the usual directive, and they exist for privileged-pipe designs
a silent vendor patch means diffing the binaries; the two changed symbols tell you which side of the boundary to look at
non_transfers: callers that pass `--` or use an argv array with the program itself exempted from parsing

evidence.target: MikroTik RouterOS SSH login path (CVE-2026-86060, 'MikroTrick' chain), fixed 7.23.4 / 7.24.2 / 6.49.21
